title: The Invention of a Shared Sign Language
summary: How Thomas Gallaudet and Laurent Clerc founded the first lasting school for deaf children in America in 1817, building a structured sign language that helped deaf people communicate and live independently.
poll: Founding a shared sign language and the first school for the deaf was one of the most important inventions for human communication.

versions.title: Talking With Your Hands
versions.text:
See those hands move fast. That is sign talk. It helps deaf kids talk.

Some kids cannot hear well. Sign talk helps them talk. It uses hands, not sound.

Long ago, deaf kids had no good way. Few schools taught sign talk. Life was hard for them.

Two men changed this. One man, Gallaudet, came from America. He met a deaf man, Clerc, in France. Clerc knew sign talk well.

The two men made a school. It was just for deaf kids. They taught kids to sign. Kids learned fast. Kids made new friends.

This new school became a model. Many schools copied it.

Now, sign talk helps many deaf kids. Kids use it in school. Adults use it at work. Some use it each day.

Sign talk gives deaf people freedom. It helps people say what they want.

versions.title: Talking With Your Hands
versions.text:
Sign language is talk with hands. It helps deaf people talk. Some people cannot hear well. Sign language lets them talk with others.

Long ago, deaf people had no good way to talk. Few schools taught sign language.

In 1817, two men in America changed this. One man, Gallaudet, met a deaf man in France. His friend, Clerc, knew sign language well.

Together, they opened a school for deaf kids. It taught kids to sign. It was not like other schools. It was easy to learn once kids started.

This new school became a model. Most deaf schools still copy it today.

Sign language now helps millions of deaf people. Kids use it to learn in school. Adults use it to talk at work. Many people sign every day.

Sign language gives deaf people real freedom. They let people say what they want.

versions.title: Talking With Your Hands
versions.text:
Sign language is a way to talk with hands, faces, and body shapes at the same time. It helps people who cannot hear well talk with others around them.

Long ago, deaf people had no good way to talk. This made going to school very hard for them.

In 1817, two men in America changed this. One man, Thomas Gallaudet, had met a deaf teacher in France. His friend, Laurent Clerc, was a skilled teacher. He liked to teach new signs.

Together, the two friends opened a school. It taught deaf children to sign in a clear way. It was built on ideas from France, not just random hand waves. This made it much easier to teach others.

This new school became the model most deaf schools follow today, two hundred years later.

Sign language now helps millions of deaf people. People use it to learn in school, to talk at work, and to chat with friends and family.

Sign language gives deaf people real freedom. They let people choose how to talk.

versions.title: Talking With Your Hands
versions.text:
Sign language is a way to talk using hands and faces. A person does not need sound at all to be understood.

Long ago, deaf people had no good way to talk with others. This made going to school, and simply living each day, hard for them.

In 1817, two men in America built something new. Gallaudet had traveled and met a deaf teacher named Clerc in France, and Clerc agreed to come teach in America. Clerc was a gifted teacher who loved his work.

Working together, the two men taught deaf children to sign in a clear, shared way. It was built on real sign language, not just made-up hand waves. Students learned quickly once they truly started.

This clever teaching idea became a lasting model. Many schools still follow it today, two hundred years later.

Sign language now helps millions of people live full lives. People use it to learn in school, to talk at work, and to video call friends and family.

Sign language gives people a real, lasting freedom. It lets a person decide how to talk and what to say.

versions.title: A School Built on Sign Language
versions.text:
Sign language is a way to talk using hands and faces. A person does not need sound to be understood at all.

For a long time, deaf people had no reliable way to talk with others. This made school and everyday life especially difficult.

An American man named Thomas Gallaudet traveled to Europe in the early 1800s. There, he met a deaf teacher named Laurent Clerc and saw the value of sign language firsthand. Clerc, a skilled teacher, agreed to help design something better.

Working together, Gallaudet and Clerc opened a school for deaf children in Connecticut in 1817. It was built from real sign language, not simple hand waves. It was much easier to teach and to learn.

That school's teaching method became the plan that deaf schools still follow, two hundred years later.

Today, sign language is used worldwide, across dozens of forms. Deaf people rely on it to attend school, hold jobs, travel, and chat with friends and family.

Many deaf people now use video calls too. A caller signs on screen, and the words come through with no sound needed. Other callers rely on live captions typed by hand.

More than anything, sign language means freedom: choosing how to talk and what to say next.

versions.title: A School Built on Sign Language
versions.text:
Sign language is a visual way to talk, using hands, faces, and body shapes. It lets people communicate without needing to speak or hear at all. For countless people, it is the everyday tool that makes independent talk possible.

Deaf people once had no reliable method for communicating independently, which made both schooling and everyday life especially difficult for them and their families.

An American man named Thomas Gallaudet traveled to Europe in the early 1800s to study teaching methods. While there, he met a skilled deaf teacher named Laurent Clerc and saw its value firsthand. Clerc, a determined educator, agreed to help design something more complete.

Working closely together, Gallaudet and Clerc opened a school for deaf children in Connecticut in 1817. It was built from real sign language, not invented hand waves, and it was much easier to teach, to learn, and to spread widely to new cities.

That teaching method eventually became the blueprint most deaf schools still follow, more than two hundred years later, from small towns to large cities nationwide.

Today, sign language helps millions of people worldwide lead full, active, genuinely independent lives. People rely on it to attend school, hold demanding careers, travel, and compete through signed storytelling and theater.

Many deaf people now also rely on video calling, letting a caller sign on screen so meaning comes through with no sound needed at all. Other callers depend on live captions typed by trained relay workers, especially during phone calls or public events like meetings.

Sign language represents real freedom and independence: the simple ability to choose, without help, how to talk and what to say next.

versions.title: The Invention of a Shared Sign Language
versions.text:
Sign language is a visual language that uses hands, facial expressions, and body shapes. It is arranged so a person can communicate fully without needing to speak or hear at all. For countless people, it is the everyday tool that makes independent communication possible.

Ways of signing have existed for a long time across many places, from small deaf communities to royal courts. Early records depict isolated, informal attempts at visual communication. Those early systems, though, were rarely shared. They were nearly impossible to teach widely or standardize.

Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet was born in the United States in 1787. He traveled to Europe seeking better methods for teaching deaf children and met Laurent Clerc, a gifted deaf teacher, in Paris. Clerc understood the power of structured sign language firsthand and agreed to help.

Collaborating closely over many months, Gallaudet and Clerc founded a school for deaf children in Connecticut in 1817, a groundbreaking achievement at the time. It was built from real, structured sign language rather than invented gestures. It proved far easier to teach and to standardize across many classrooms.

That teaching model ultimately became the blueprint that most deaf schools continue to follow, even today, shaping language programs from America to countries worldwide.

Today, sign language helps millions of people lead full, independent lives. People depend on it to attend school, hold careers, travel, and connect through theater and storytelling.

Many deaf people now also rely on video calling, letting a caller sign on screen so meaning comes through with no sound required. Other callers rely on live captions typed by trained relay workers.

Whichever tool a person uses today, the basic idea stays the same: sign language should let a person communicate at a natural pace, rather than depending on someone else to translate every single word.

Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet was born in the United States in 1787. He traveled to Europe seeking better methods for teaching deaf children and met Laurent Clerc, a gifted deaf teacher, in Paris. keyWords.example: Her firsthand knowledge of the storm helped her warn the neighbors.

keyWords.definition: to make something follow one consistent set of rules everywhere
keyWords.example: The committee worked for years to standardize the spelling rules used in every textbook.

keyWords.definition: carefully organized according to a clear, consistent system
keyWords.example: The coach introduced a more structured practice schedule for the team.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of this article?
options: Sign language is only ever useful for formal theater performances
Gallaudet and Clerc's partnership produced a structured method that became the enduring standard
Sign language has remained completely unchanged since ancient times
Deaf communities never developed any way to communicate before 1817
questions.why: The article centers on how Gallaudet and Clerc's partnership produced a structured teaching method that became the enduring standard for deaf education.

wrong.A: The article describes uses in school, careers, and travel, not only theater.
wrong.C: The article explicitly describes a major development in 1817.
wrong.D: The article describes earlier, isolated sign systems that existed before 1817.

questions.stem: According to the article, how did Laurent Clerc's personal background shape the school's approach?
options: He had never actually taught another person before this
He designed the entire method purely from distant academic research
He had no real personal connection to deaf communities at all
His own experience as a deaf person gave him firsthand insight into structured sign language
questions.why: The article explains that Clerc, as a deaf teacher, understood the power of structured sign language firsthand.

wrong.A: The article describes him as a gifted, experienced deaf teacher.
wrong.B: The article credits personal experience, not distant academic research alone.
wrong.C: The article explicitly describes his deep personal connection.

questions.stem: What evidence suggests earlier sign systems were genuinely limited, not simply undocumented?
options: They were far too small to ever be printed clearly in books
They required an unusual amount of natural sunlight to use
They were isolated, informal, and nearly impossible to teach widely or standardize
They were brightly painted and somewhat difficult to clean
questions.why: The article specifically cites the isolated, informal nature of earlier systems as evidence of their real limitations.

wrong.A: Printing in books is not the article's framing of sign language.
wrong.B: Sign language relies on sight, not sunlight specifically.
wrong.D: Paint or cleaning is not discussed in the article.

questions.stem: Why does the article emphasize that Gallaudet and Clerc tested their methods repeatedly?
options: To argue that careful testing of new methods was actually unnecessary
To show that achieving a reliable teaching method required careful effort, not luck
To suggest that their final method ultimately turned out to be a failure
To prove that teaching deaf children is an unusually dangerous task
questions.why: Emphasizing repeated testing highlights that the breakthrough came from deliberate effort rather than chance.

wrong.A: The article clearly values the careful testing process.
wrong.C: The article presents the final method as a lasting success.
wrong.D: Danger is not discussed anywhere in the article.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why the school's model spread to other regions over time?
options: It was only ever used by a small group of professional performers
It was required everywhere by a brand-new international law
No other schools for the deaf were ever built again after this one
It likely solved a problem that many deaf communities shared across different places
questions.why: Since the model became the widely followed blueprint, it likely solved a shared problem across many different deaf communities.

wrong.A: The article mentions many everyday uses, not only performance.
wrong.B: No such law is mentioned anywhere in the article.
wrong.C: The article describes many schools that still exist today.

questions.stem: In this article, what does the word standardize most likely mean?
options: To make something follow one consistent set of rules everywhere
To make something far more expensive to produce overall
To remove a plan entirely and leave no structure behind
To make a method impossible for anyone else to teach
questions.why: Standardize means to make something follow one consistent set of rules everywhere, which is what happened as the method spread to new schools.

wrong.B: Cost is not related to the word's meaning.
wrong.C: Standardize is closer to creating consistent structure, not removing it.
wrong.D: The article shows standardizing made teaching easier, not impossible.

questions.stem: How does the article primarily structure its account of the school's development?
options: By presenting two opposing viewpoints without any real resolution
By listing a series of unrelated facts about France generally
By tracing a problem through a specific solution to its lasting modern impact
By comparing several completely unrelated writing systems
questions.why: The article moves from the limitations of earlier sign systems, to Gallaudet and Clerc's specific solution, to its continuing influence today.

wrong.A: No opposing viewpoints are presented in the article.
wrong.B: The facts connect into one developing story, not an unrelated list.
wrong.D: No unrelated writing systems are compared in the article.

questions.stem: Based on the article, which outcome most directly resulted from the school's structured method?
options: Teaching quickly became the only career ever open to deaf people
Millions of deaf people gained a dependable way to communicate and live independently
Spoken language became completely unnecessary for most people
All schools everywhere switched entirely to video calls within years
questions.why: The article directly credits the structured method with giving deaf people a dependable, independent way to communicate.

wrong.A: The article does not claim teaching became the only career available.
wrong.C: Spoken language is not discussed as unnecessary.
wrong.D: Video calls are described as a modern addition, not an immediate switch.

HIGH.prompt: Analyze how the article uses evidence about both the limitations of earlier sign systems and Gallaudet and Clerc's partnership to explain why their method became the enduring standard.
checklist: Analyzes the documented limitations of earlier, informal sign systems
Explains how Gallaudet and Clerc's complementary backgrounds shaped their solution
Connects their work to its lasting influence on deaf communities today
HIGH.modelAnswer: Before 1817, ways of signing existed across many isolated communities, but they remained informal, rarely shared, and nearly impossible to teach widely or standardize. Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet, an American educator, traveled to Europe seeking real educational methods and met Laurent Clerc, a deaf teacher who understood the power of structured sign language firsthand. Collaborating closely, the two men founded a school for deaf children in Connecticut in 1817, testing their teaching methods repeatedly until each lesson worked as intended, building the school on real, structured sign language rather than invented gestures. This structured approach proved far easier to teach and to standardize, and it ultimately became the blueprint that most deaf schools worldwide continue to follow, giving millions of people a dependable way to communicate and live independently, now often supplemented by video calling and trained relay workers.

LOW.stem: What can you tell about how the new school changed daily life for deaf kids?
options: It likely made talking much easier
It likely made talking much harder
It had no effect on talking at all
It only worked outside
LOW.why: Since the school taught real sign language, it likely made talking much easier for deaf kids.

wrong.B: The text shows the new school solved a problem, not created one.
wrong.C: The text clearly shows talking changed because of the school.
wrong.D: No outdoor-only limit is mentioned.

LOW.stem: Why is 1817 an important year in this story?
options: It is when Gallaudet and Clerc opened their school
It is when sign language was first invented ever
It is when France stopped teaching deaf kids
It is when video calls were invented
LOW.why: The text says Gallaudet and Clerc opened their school in 1817.

wrong.B: Sign language existed in some form before 1817.
wrong.C: France teaching deaf kids stopping is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Video call invention is not discussed.

LOW.stem: Why does the story explain that deaf people had no good way to talk before the school?
options: To show why the new school was such an important change
To explain how to build a house
To describe a different, unrelated invention
To list facts with no connection
LOW.why: Describing the old problem helps readers understand why the new school was such an important change.

wrong.B: Building houses in general is not the topic.
wrong.C: The old problem is directly related, not unrelated.
wrong.D: The facts connect to build one clear story.

LOW.stem: What is the effect of the school using real sign language instead of made-up waves?
options: Kids learned to talk much faster
Kids learned to talk much slower
Kids could no longer talk at all
It cost nothing to build the school
LOW.why: The text says using real sign language helped kids learn to talk much faster.

wrong.B: The text says the opposite; kids learned faster.
wrong.C: Kids could still talk, as shown throughout the story.
wrong.D: Cost is not discussed in the story.

MID.stem: What is the most likely reason the article explains the problems deaf people faced before this school existed?
options: To help readers understand why the new method was such an important improvement
To give a full history of French schools
To compare sign language with spoken language
To explain how video calls work
MID.why: Describing the earlier problems helps readers understand just how significant Gallaudet and Clerc's improvement really was.

wrong.B: French school history in general is not the article's focus.
wrong.C: Spoken language is not compared in detail.
wrong.D: Video calls are only mentioned as a modern addition.

MID.stem: If Clerc had not been a deaf teacher himself, what does the article suggest might have happened?
options: He might not have understood sign language's value as deeply
The school would have opened in exactly the same way
Nothing about the story would change at all
Gallaudet would have built the school completely alone
MID.why: Since the article credits his personal experience with helping him understand sign language's value, lacking that experience might have changed his understanding of the problem.

wrong.B: The article implies his experience mattered, so this seems unlikely.
wrong.C: His personal experience is presented as directly relevant.
wrong.D: The article describes the two men working together, not alone.

MID.stem: How does the article's final paragraph support its main point?
options: It shows the long-term impact that grew out of the school's method
It introduces an entirely new, unrelated topic
It contradicts facts given earlier in the article
It simply repeats the opening sentence word for word
MID.why: The ending connects the school's method to its lasting impact on communication today, reinforcing the article's main point.

wrong.B: The ending stays on the topic of the method's impact.
wrong.C: The ending supports, rather than contradicts, earlier details.
wrong.D: The ending adds new information about lasting impact, not a repeated sentence.

MID.stem: Which word from the article is closest in meaning to independent?
options: Self-reliant
Isolated
Relay
Educator
MID.why: Independent means able to act on one's own, which is close in meaning to self-reliant.

wrong.B: Isolated describes being cut off, not independence.
wrong.C: Relay describes passing a message, not independence.
wrong.D: Educator describes a job, not independence.

HIGH.stem: Which claim would the article most strongly support with evidence?
options: The lasting value of the school depended on combining teaching skill with lived experience of deafness
Only hearing teachers can truly understand deaf education
Mechanical engineering played the central role in sign language's spread
The teaching method has remained completely unused since 1817
HIGH.why: The article's evidence, that Clerc's firsthand deaf experience combined with Gallaudet's educational drive produced the breakthrough, supports the idea that combining teaching skill with lived experience was essential.

wrong.B: The article centers a deaf teacher's firsthand insight as essential, contradicting this claim.
wrong.C: Mechanical engineering is not discussed in this article.
wrong.D: The article states the method is still followed today.

HIGH.stem: What is the most likely reason the article contrasts earlier isolated sign systems with Gallaudet and Clerc's structured method?
options: To highlight exactly what made their method a genuine breakthrough
To argue that earlier deaf communities were entirely incapable of communication
To prove that France invented all sign language alone
To suggest the school was built with no real planning
HIGH.why: Contrasting the isolated, informal earlier systems with the later structured method highlights precisely what made the 1817 breakthrough so meaningful.

wrong.B: The article does not dismiss earlier communities as incapable, just limited in standardization.
wrong.C: The article credits both an American and a Frenchman, not France alone.
wrong.D: The article describes careful, repeated testing, not a lack of planning.

HIGH.stem: Based on the article, which best explains why Gallaudet and Clerc's method became so influential?
options: It was the first method to combine structure with teachability, leading to widespread adoption
It was invented by a government health agency
It replaced the need for any physical communication at all
It was the only teaching method ever created for any subject
HIGH.why: The article credits the method's lasting influence to its unprecedented combination of structure and teachability, which led to widespread adoption as the standard.

wrong.B: The article credits two individuals, not a government agency.
wrong.C: The article does not claim it replaced physical communication generally.
wrong.D: The article clearly describes it as specific to deaf education.

HIGH.stem: Which word pair from the article are most closely related in meaning?
options: Isolated and informal
Firsthand and relay
Structured and groundbreaking
Educator and standardize
HIGH.why: Isolated and informal both describe the scattered, unstandardized qualities of earlier sign systems, so they are closely related in meaning.

wrong.B: Firsthand describes direct experience, while relay describes passing a message; these describe different things.
wrong.C: Structured describes organization, while groundbreaking describes novelty; related but not synonyms.
wrong.D: An educator is a person, while to standardize is an action; these are different kinds of words.
